issues.legal_issue: A declared market area is invalid for excessive breadth only when its scope makes effective regulation or convenient access to the market yards unreasonable.
material_facts: The government declared an area to be a market area after considering objections and suggestions.
The challengers offered no material showing that sales and purchases could not be effectively controlled or that growers could not conveniently bring their produce to the market yards.
issues.conclusion: The declaration was not shown to be unreasonable or invalid because of the area’s breadth.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 4(1) of the Bihar Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1960, the government must exercise its power to declare a market area reasonably after considering objections and suggestions. The court found no basis on the record for holding that the area was so wide as to prevent effective control or convenient access; it relied on no earlier case for this issue.

rule.if: market_area_challenge and declaration_followed_consideration_of_objections and not evidence_of_ineffective_control and not evidence_of_inconvenient_access

predicates.market_area_challenge: The proceeding challenges the breadth of an area declared for regulation of agricultural produce markets.
predicates.declaration_followed_consideration_of_ob: The government considered objections and suggestions before declaring the area.
predicates.evidence_of_ineffective_control: The challenger showed that the area’s breadth prevents effective control of sales and purchases.
predicates.evidence_of_inconvenient_access: The challenger showed that growers cannot conveniently bring their produce to the market yards.

issues.definition: When an area declaration is challenged for breadth, consideration of objections and the absence of evidence of ineffective control or inconvenient access mean the declaration is not unreasonable for breadth.

issues.legal_issue: A market may be established by defining its market proper and market yards without providing a separate, fully equipped market site, unless the government has directed the committee to provide particular facilities.
material_facts: The market committee recommended boundaries for the market proper and the principal and sub-market yards.
The government issued notifications declaring the market proper and the market yards.
It was not shown that the committee had refused to carry out a government direction to provide facilities.
The committee was not required to acquire land or buildings for the market.
issues.conclusion: The market was established through the prescribed notifications, and the absence of a separate equipped site did not invalidate its establishment.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(h), 5(2), and 18(i) of the Bihar Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1960, read with rule 59, provide for establishment of a market by defining the market proper and market yards through the prescribed process. Section 18(i) requires the committee to provide facilities that the government directs; sections 28(2) and 30(i) permit acquisition of land and buildings but do not make it obligatory. The definition of a market does not require a separate site equipped with facilities.

rule.if: market_establishment_challenge and committee_recommended_market_boundaries and government_notified_market_boundaries and not committee_refused_directed_facilities

predicates.market_establishment_challenge: The proceeding challenges whether a regulated agricultural produce market has been established.
predicates.committee_recommended_market_boundaries: The market committee recommended boundaries for the market proper and the market yards.
predicates.government_notified_market_boundaries: The government issued notifications defining the market proper and the market yards.
predicates.committee_refused_directed_facilities: The market committee refused to provide facilities that the government directed it to provide.

issues.definition: In a challenge to market establishment, committee recommendations and government notifications defining the market boundaries establish the market without a separate equipped site if the committee has not refused directed facilities.

issues.legal_issue: Market and licence fees are valid fees rather than taxes when they are not excessive, are connected to services for market users, and are set apart for the statutory market purposes.
material_facts: The committee took steps to bring buyers and sellers together and regulate sales at fair prices.
It worked to eliminate unhealthy practices, define and prohibit improper charges, and ensure correct weighing and measuring.
It provided for dispute resolution, price and market information, grading instruction, standard contracts, and enforcement staff.
The levies were correlated with expenses for those services, were not excessive, and were placed in a fund earmarked for statutory purposes.
issues.conclusion: The market and licence fees were supported by sufficient quid pro quo and satisfied the test for fees.
issues.legal_principle: The market fee was levied under section 27 read with rule 61, and licence fees were prescribed under sections 18(ii) and rules 71 and 73 of the Bihar Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1960 and the Bihar Agricultural Produce Market Rules, 1962. The court applied the fee test in Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt, [1954] S.C.R. 1005: the levies must have sufficient quid pro quo in services and benefits connected with their collection.

rule.if: market_levy_challenge and committee_provided_market_services and levies_correlated_with_service_costs and levies_not_excessive and levy_fund_earmarked_for_market_purposes

predicates.market_levy_challenge: The proceeding challenges levies imposed in connection with a regulated agricultural produce market.
predicates.committee_provided_market_services: The market committee provided services and facilities connected with the regulated market.
predicates.levies_correlated_with_service_costs: The levies were related to expenses incurred in providing the services.
predicates.levies_not_excessive: The amounts of the levies were not excessive.
predicates.levy_fund_earmarked_for_market_purposes: The collected money was set apart for the statutory purposes of the market.

issues.definition: For a market-levy challenge, non-excessive levies connected to committee services, related to their costs, and earmarked for market purposes are valid fees.

issues.legal_issue: Gradual implementation of a market-regulation scheme in different areas does not, by itself, violate equality merely because the scheme has not yet been implemented throughout the state.
material_facts: The government had implemented the market-regulation scheme in some areas but not throughout the state.
The government could establish regulated markets in different parts of the state gradually and from time to time.
issues.conclusion: The government was not required to implement the Act and Rules throughout the state at the same time, and implementation in one area did not on that basis violate equality.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 of the Constitution does not require the state to implement the Bihar Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1960 and its Rules in all areas simultaneously. The state may establish regulated markets in different areas gradually and from time to time. The court relied on no earlier case for this issue.

predicates.equality_challenge_to_market_implementat: The proceeding alleges unequal treatment because a market-regulation scheme has been implemented in some areas but not others.
predicates.scheme_implemented_in_some_areas: The government has implemented the market-regulation scheme in at least one area.
predicates.scheme_implemented_gradually: The government is introducing regulated markets in different areas over time.

issues.definition: When an equality challenge rests on implementation in only some areas, gradual implementation means that the difference alone does not violate equality.

issues.legal_issue: A licensing rule requiring operators to obtain licences for business in a market is not invalid on the ground that it imposes a licensing requirement throughout the wider market area when the rule has been amended to apply to the market instead.
material_facts: An earlier version of the licensing rule required licences for operating throughout the market area and was held by the High Court to exceed the statutory authority.
The rules were amended by substituting “market” for “market area.”
issues.conclusion: The amendment cured the objection that the licensing rules exceeded the authority conferred by the Act.
issues.legal_principle: Section 18(ii) of the Bihar Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1960 authorizes a licensing requirement for persons doing business in a market. Rules 71 and 73 were amended so that the licensing obligation applied to the market rather than the entire market area. The court relied on Thakur Prasad Gupta v. The State of Bihar, which had struck down the earlier rule for extending the obligation throughout the market area.

predicates.licensing_rule_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity of a rule requiring market operators to obtain licences.
predicates.rule_requires_licence_for_market_busines: The rule requires a person doing business as a market operator to obtain a licence.
predicates.rule_limited_to_market_not_wider_area: The licensing requirement is limited to business in the market rather than business throughout a broader regulated area.

issues.definition: A challenged licensing rule requiring a licence for market business is not invalid for exceeding statutory authority when its scope is limited to the market rather than a wider area.
